transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-02-11
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Anita Rao (CISO, Summit Financial), Mark Holden (Cloud Architect), Priya Singh (IT Security), Evan Lee (Procurement)

Auto-summary: Security deep dive focused on Private/VPC deployment, network isolation, ingress/egress, firewalling, and compliance artifacts.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out the hour. Maya from Redwood here, i'm the AE on the account. Luis and Samir are our security/arch SEs. Anita, Mark, Priya, thanks for joining — should we quickly do intros?
[00:25] Anita: Hi all, Anita Rao, CISO for Summit Financial. We're evaluating private deployments for sensitive customer PII workloads. Primary concerns: network isolation, auditability, and key management.
[00:40] Mark: Mark Holden, cloud architect. I'll own the VPC design and peering.
[00:48] Priya: Priya Singh, IT security. Focused on firewalling, egress controls, and DLP boundaries.
[00:55] Maya: Great. Quick agenda: walk through our recommended private VPC topology, ingress/egress patterns, firewall/NACL suggestions, SSO/KMS integration, and then Q&A and next steps.
[01:15] Luis: I'll start with a high-level of how Redwood's private deployment sits in a customer VPC — we offer a control plane that can be customer-managed and a data plane that lives in your VPC or your on-prem network depending on the pattern.
[01:35] Mark: Question — is the control plane outside our network entirely for the managed option? We need to understand data paths and ports.
[01:45] Samir: For the hosted-control pattern the control plane is in Redwood's cloud, but the data plane can be fully inside your VPC. For the private package we can run both control + data in a customer-managed VPC or an on-prem cluster; options are flexible. Control plane-to-data plane traffic uses mutual TLS and port 8443 by default, but we can customize.
[02:20] Anita: Can you say more about ingress? We need to prevent internet-facing endpoints for inference.
[02:30] Luis: Absolutely — two common patterns: 1) Internal-only endpoints behind a private ALB with internal DN and 2) On-prem gateway that tunnels to the data plane. For internal ALB we recommend no public listeners; access via private peering or Transit Gateway.
[03:00] Priya: For the ALB approach, how do you suggest we handle egress to third-party telemetry or updates? We need strict egress allowlists.
[03:15] Samir: We surface explicit egress IPs for our service (a small range) that you can allowlist. Alternatively, you can rout egress through a NAT gateway and restrict destination IPs in your firewall. We also support routing updates via a customer-managed proxy.
[03:40] Mark: About peering — do you require direct VPC peering, or can we use Transit Gateway? Our org prefers transit for centralised routing.
[03:55] Luis: Transit Gateway is supported. We recommend TGW in front of the Redwood subnets so you get centralized routing and egress inspection. Avoid cross-region peering for sensitive workloads unless you explicitly need multi-region failover.
[04:20] Anita: How about east-west segmentation inside the VPC? We don't want the Redwood subnets to talk to other app subnets.
[04:30] Samir: Make Redwood subnets their own security domain: separate subnets, stricter NACLs, and SGs that only allow ranges from your API tiers. Default SG should be deny-all inbound and minimally permissive outbound to telemetry destinations.
[04:55] Priya: Are there any required host-level ports for the inference hosts? Our security team insists on a port inventory.
[05:05] Luis: Main ports: 22 for optional SSH to bastion (we recommend agent-based management instead), 443 for HTTPS, 8443 for internal control plane comms, and gRPC ports for internal inter-service — we'll provide a full port list. We also support ephemeral ports for KV cache sync which we document.
[05:40] Mark: You mentioned KV cache — do you mean KV cache replication across instances? Any chance that's open to misinterpretation as "KV cash" in our docs ; )
[05:50] Samir: [laughs] Yes KV cache, not cash. There are small windows where nodes exchange cache state. We can pin that to an internal VPC CIDR and SG to tighten it.
[06:10] Anita: Data residency: we need logs and raw request payloads to stay in our VPC. Does Redwood store anything outside my VPC in private deployment?
[06:25] Luis: For a private deployment with customer-managed data plane, raw requests and model state remain in your VPC. Control plane metadata can be routed to Redwood's control plane if you choose managed control plane; otherwise you can host the control plane in your VPC to keep everything internal.
[06:50] Priya: Encryption and KMS — can we use our existing AWS KMS/HSM for model keys and token encryption?
[07:00] Samir: Yes — we support integrating with customer KMS (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, or on-prem HSM). Keys for at-rest encryption and envelope keys for any exported artifacts can be customer-managed. We recommend an IAM role with least privilege for KMS decrypt.
[07:30] Mark: For audit logs, do you push to CloudWatch/Log Insights or can we send to our SIEM?
[07:40] Luis: We can stream audit logs to CloudWatch, Stackdriver, or a syslog endpoint. For SIEMs, we recommend forwarding from CloudWatch -> Kinesis -> SIEM. Immutable logs can also be stored in an S3 bucket with Object Lock for compliance.
[08:05] Anita: SOC2 artifacts: do you have a SOC 2 Type II and ISO attestation? We'll need the reports for procurement.
[08:15] Maya: Yes, we have both. We'll send the latest SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 attestations. We'll redact any customer-sensitive info before sharing.
[08:30] Evan: On procurement, any standard contractual clauses around data residency? We have EEA customers.
[08:40] Maya: We support region-specific private deployments; you can restrict the data plane to a given region. We'll include the region options in the follow-up.
[08:55] Mark: Firewalling specifics — are you recommending stateful security groups or NACLs for layer defense?
[09:05] Samir: Use both: security groups as primary host-level controls (stateful) and NACLs for subnet-level stateless filtering to block known bad ranges. Put stricter deny rules at the NACL level for outbound to telemetry endpoints unless explicitly allowed.
[09:35] Priya: Any recommended rules for blocking data exfil via DNS or nonstandard ports?
[09:45] Luis: Block all outbound DNS except to your internal resolvers. Use DNS logging/inspection and force outbound DNS to an internal DNS proxy. Also block outbound to uncommon ports and implement egress rules that are destination/IP based.
[10:10] Anita: SSO and RBAC — we want SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning, plus fine-grained RBAC for model access and route-level controls.
[10:25] Samir: We support SAML and OIDC for SSO, SCIM for provisioning, and RBAC with resource-level roles (model-admin, route-admin, auditor). Audit logs capture token-level operations and model deployments.
[10:50] Mark: Are tokens short-lived? We prefer no long-lived credentials in the app plane.
[10:58] Luis: We use short-lived session tokens and recommend rotating service credentials regularly. For machine-to-machine, use short TTLs with a refresh flow, and back that with KMS for key wrapping.
[11:20] Priya: Pen tests — do you do external penetration tests on the private deployment package?
[11:30] Maya: Yes, we run annual penetration tests and will share the executive summary and remediation items.
[11:40] Evan: For on-prem deployments, what network prerequisites do we need? VLANs, firewall rules, NAT?
[11:50] Samir: VLANs for segmentation, a management VLAN for orchestration plane, isolated compute VLANs for inference, and a dedicated egress appliance for updates. We recommend a small NAT pool for outbound connections and strict ACLs on the edge firewall.
[12:20] Mark: We have an existing IDS/IPS — can Redwood send traces or sidecar logs to it?
[12:30] Luis: Yes — we can export telemetry via syslog or a sidecar that sends to your IDS. There's also a prometheus exporter for metrics if you want to ingest observability signals.
[12:50] Anita: What about patching and host management? We can't have deferred patches for security reasons.
[13:00] Samir: For on-prem we provide an image and a documented patch schedule; we can integrate with your patch management tooling so you control patch windows. For managed data plane, we handle OS/kernel patches in coordination with your maintenance windows.
[13:25] Maya: Quick pause — any show-stoppers so far?
[13:30] Anita: Not yet. Just need to validate the network diagrams and confirm the KMS integration specifics.
[13:40] Mark: Also want to understand expected egress throughput — our gateway caps at certain rates for third-party destinations.
[13:50] Luis: We should run a bench test — we'll propose a simple throughput profile and you'll validate in your pre-prod. That's one of the next steps.
[14:10] Priya: About logging retention — required for us is 7 years for certain financial logs. Can Redwood support long-term immutable retention of audit logs?
[14:25] Samir: We can ship logs to your S3 with Lifecycle rules and Object Lock for write-once. Retention policies can be configured by your compliance team.
[14:40] Maya: Let's talk about ingress TLS termination — do you prefer customer-managed certs or Redwood-managed certs for the internal ALB?
[14:50] Luis: Customer-managed certs are preferable for internal compliance. We support certs in ACM or external cert managers; we also integrate with vault for cert rotation if you need.
[15:10] Mark: For network monitoring, we want flow logs — VPC Flow Logs, but also host-level connections.
[15:20] Samir: VPC Flow Logs for macro traffic patterns and host-level auditing via auditd or agent that forwards to your SIEM. We can surface connection-level logs for all inference requests.
[15:40] Anita: A slightly thorny issue: will Redwood ever cache or persist decrypted payloads? We can't allow that.
[15:50] Luis: We do not persist decrypted payloads in managed customer data plane. Any in-memory processing is ephemeral; for debug-only mode you can explicitly enable request dumps but it's off by default.
[16:10] Priya: How do you secure backups, snapshots of model artifacts which may contain customer data?
[16:20] Samir: Backups are encrypted with customer-managed keys and stored in your region. Snapshot access is audited and restricted to specific service accounts. We recommend rotating snapshot keys regularly.
[16:45] Mark: For transit encryption between nodes, is mTLS used everywhere?
[16:55] Luis: Yes, mutual TLS with cert rotation. We can integrate with your PKI or manage certs internally; best practice is customer PKI for highest control.
[17:15] Maya: A couple of notes on firewalling patterns we recommend: default deny, whitelist only required management IPs, deploy an egress proxy for telemetry, and use TGW for centralized routing. We'll circulate a hardened rulebook.
[17:40] Anita: Could you include recommended NACL entries and example security group manifests? That will speed our security review.
[17:50] Maya: Absolutely, that's in our action items.
[18:00] Mark: Do you require any inbound from the internet for updates or license checks?
[18:10] Samir: No mandatory inbound. Updates can be pulled via egress to allowlisted endpoints or staged through your internal mirror repository. License checks are optional and can be offline.
[18:35] Priya: Regarding egress IP ranges — can you give us a small static set? Our perimeter firewall team dislikes dynamic ranges.
[18:45] Luis: We'll provide a small CIDR block list for the managed services and for the private package we'll provide the sample egress pool you can assign. When you host in your VPC the egress IPs are yours.
[19:10] Maya: Let's cover RBAC a bit more — can we map your roles to our SSO groups?
[19:20] Samir: Yes, SCIM mapping is supported so groups map to roles. We also support a read-only auditor role and can restrict model delete permissions to a small admin group.
[19:40] Anita: Audit log tamper-proofing — are logs immutable?
[19:50] Luis: We recommend S3 Object Lock with Write Once Read Many (WORM) to prevent tampering, plus cross-account replication for redundancy.
[20:05] Mark: For on-prem HSM, any vendor certs you validated? We use Thales.
[20:15] Samir: We have integration templates for Thales and recommended connection diagrams. We'll include example policy bindings.
[20:40] Priya: Anything about IDS alert signatures or false positives from model telemetry? We want to avoid noisy alerts.
[20:50] Luis: We can tune telemetry granularity and provide a suppression profile that filters model heartbeat and known benign patterns.
[21:10] Anita: If something goes wrong, incident response — do you provide runbooks and a postmortem SLA?
[21:20] Maya: Yes, incident runbooks and an escalations matrix are part of our enterprise support. We'll share the runbook and an SLO for incident acknowledgement times.
[21:40] Evan: Procurement question: service-level indemnities for data breaches?
[21:50] Maya: We'll put standard indemnities in a draft SOW; legal can follow up. We'll include SOC2 as part of the attachment.
[22:10] Mark: Network latency — can you bind inference routing to local AZ subnets to minimize cross-AZ traffic?
[22:20] Samir: Yes, we support AZ-local placement of compute and local routing tables to reduce cross-AZ hops.
[22:40] Priya: How do you recommend we test ingress/egress rules before production rollout?
[22:50] Luis: Deploy in a pre-prod VPC mirrored to prod but with lower scale, run synthetic traffic and egress bench tests, and validate SIEM/IDS logs. We'll help script the tests.
[23:10] Anita: Ok — please include step-by-step of the bench test and expected metrics.
[23:20] Luis: We'll include sample scripts, expected CPU/RPS curves, and egress throughput numbers.
[23:35] Maya: We're nearing 25 minutes in — any deep technical dives left?
[23:40] Mark: One last one — cross-account access for our dev teams. We want separate AWS accounts with read-only visibility.
[23:50] Samir: We support cross-account roles and a dedicated auditor role for cross-account visibility without write perms.
[24:05] Priya: Can we audit who calls a model and which prompt was used?
[24:15] Luis: Yes, audit logs include request-level metadata including calling principal and route. Request payload retention is optional and controlled by you.
[24:40] Anita: Encryption in flight — are there any exceptions for internal network traffic?
[24:50] Samir: All internal traffic is mTLS encrypted; no plain text by default.
[25:05] Maya: Let's recap next steps and owners.
[25:10] Maya: Action items: Maya send diagrams and rulebook; Luis send bench-test script; Mark provide VPC CIDRs; Anita confirm compliance owners; schedule follow-up bench test.
[26:00] Mark: We'll aim to get the CIDRs and peering diagram within a week.
[26:10] Anita: I'll coordinate the compliance questionnaire owners.
[26:20] Evan: Procurement will review SOW and ask about timelines.
[26:30] Maya: Great, we'll send the package by Monday. Any final questions?
[26:40] Priya: One micro question: are model artifacts stored encrypted at rest by default?
[26:50] Samir: Yes, by default at-rest encryption with customer-managed KMS if requested.
[27:05] Maya: Thanks all — we appreciate the time. We'll follow up with the docs and schedule the bench test.
[27:15] Anita: Thanks, talk soon.
[27:20] Mark: Thanks everyone.
[27:30] (call ends)

Notes: timestamps in transcript are approximate; some automatic transcription errors present (e.g., \"KV cash\" instead of \"KV cache\" in one utterance) as typical in meeting transcripts.
